BOOK_A.title: Automatic Litigation Representatives
BOOK_A.related_provisions: 2.19 (authority to settle) ; 2.21 (replacement of litigation representative) ; 11.7 (service on litigation representative).
BOOK_A.commentary:
If a litigant is an adult not under a disability, the court cannot appoint a litigation representative
for her, and she can speak to the court only personally or through a lawyer. A relative may give
the litigant quiet assistance and advice under R.2.23, but cannot speak for her. Rule 2.13 and a
signed power of attorney do not change that.¹
A strict common-law rule was applied, which is that a foreign executor who has not resealed
probate in Alberta cannot be a party to litigation here against the estate.²

footnotes.text: Nahirney v. Ogilvie & Co.2011 ABQB 586, 525 AR 14.
Here the Saskatchewan executors refused to attorn to the jurisdiction of Alberta: Hill v. Hill 2010 ABQB 528, 501 AR 227.

BOOK_B.title: Automatic litigation representatives

commentary.text: Rule 2.13 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.13. 1. Appointment by Instrument In Nahirney v. Ogilvie & Co., 2011 ABQB 586, 2011 CarswellAlta 2363, 525 A.R. 14, 26 C.P.C. (7th) 425, [2011] A.J. No. 1354, the Plaintiff's father sought to represent his daughter by virtue of a Power of Attorney executed by his daughter. Lee, J. said, at paragraphs 22–28: 22 Rule 2.13(e) allows a person to become an automatic litigation representative by virtue of having an instrument such as a power of attorney, However the Rule should only apply to instances in which a litigation representative is required to be appointed. If the result of Rule 2.13(e) was to allow anyone to appoint a non-lawyer as their de-facto representative in court, then s. 106 of the Legal Profession Act would be rendered meaningless. 23 The Alberta Rules of Court also contemplate a conflict with any other statutes in Rule 1.9, which reads: Conflicts and inconsistencies with enactments 1.9 Except as expressly provided, if there is a conflict or inconsistency between these rules and an enactment, the enactment prevails to the extent of the conflict or inconsistency. 24 Even if Mr. Nahirney is capable of being appointed litigation representative pursuant to the Alberta Rules of Court, he would still be prohibited from representing his daughter's interest in the litigation. The permissibility of litigation representatives to represent others in court has not been dealt with under the current Alberta Rules of Court. Our Court of Appeal has considered the use of Next Friends under the old Rules of Court in the case of a minor as follows: …[A] next friend is not a party to the lawsuit. He is an officer of the court under its control, and cannot even make a binding settlement on behalf of the infants (even as to modes of procedure). It is elementary that a non-lawyer cannot represent someone else as advocate before the superior courts. Salamon v. Alberta (Minister of Education) (1991), 120 AR 298 at para. 3. See also Torrance v. Alberta 2010 ABCA 88 at para. 14 Conclusion 25 Self represented litigants are expressly granted a right of audience before the court pursuant to Rule 2.22, … 26 The Plaintiff's father Mr. Nahirney is permitted to provide limited assistance to his daughter by virtue of Rule 2.23. … 27 Accordingly, the Ogilvie Defendants cannot object to Mr. Nahirney assisting his daughter pursuant to Rule 2.23. However Rule 2.23 does not permit Mr. Nahirney to stand in the place of a lawyer and represent his daughter. Rule 2.23 contains an explicit reference to s. 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act. The conduct of any person assisting a party before the Court must fall short of “acting as a barrister or solicitor” and “commencing, carrying on or defending an action or proceeding before a court or judge on behalf of another person”. 28 I conclude that Rule 2.11, 2.13 and 2.14(1) were intended to grant representation only in cases where a litigation representative was necessary under the Alberta Rules of Court. In the present case, the Plaintiff does not suffer from a disability and is not a minor, therefore there is no basis for the appointment of a Litigation Representative. In Champagne v. Sidorsky, 2012 ABQB 522, 2012 CarswellAlta 1437, 548 A.R. 10, Justice C. M. Jones noted at paragraph 5: 5 On November 17, 2011, Justice Hunt McDonald determined that Rule 2.13(e) should only apply in instances in which a litigation representative is required to be appointed. She determined that the appointment of Cindy and Cheri under the EPA did not automatically mean that Douglas was required or permitted to have a litigation representative.
